title: CD4+ T Cell Activating Hydrogels for Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
The proposed research seeks to apply a novel hydrogel-based platform for the in vivo expansion of tumor-
specific CD4+ T cells for adoptive cell therapy. Using this platform, we will examine how several significant
physicochemical and biomolecular factors influence the anti-tumor function of antigen-specific cytotoxic CD4+
T cells and co-cultured helper CD4+ and cytotoxic CD8+ T cells. We will also adapt this technology to expand
human tumor-specific CD4+ T cells to demonstrate the clinical relevance of this technology.

title: Enhancing Surveillance Methods for Genomic Epidemiology in Healthcare
text:
Current methods of detecting healthcare-associated infection (HAI) outbreaks rely on outdated, reactive
approaches that are inaccurate and often miss multiple outbreaks. This project will lead to: 1) an enhanced
understanding of HAI transmission dynamics within healthcare environments; 2) a comprehensive understanding
of the risks of transmission and acquisition of HAIs; and 3) strategies to halt and prevent outbreaks altogether.
The application of these findings can result in the reduction of high-morbidity and mortality infections, improving
patient safety and providing additional research avenues for future studies on healthcare outbreaks.

title: Engineering circularly structured guide RNA for sustained CRISPRi-mediated suppression of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis drivers.
text:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic, progressive lung disease with an unknown cause; currently, lung
transplantation is the only treatment that addresses lung damage and improves quality of life. This study aims to
develop a safe, effective therapeutic approach to inhibit drivers of fibrosis in the lung, and assess the impact on
disease pathways and outcomes in mouse and human models of IPF. This work will reveal key insights into the
biology of IPF, and inform the development of a sustained gene-silencing treatment for IPF and other lung
diseases.

title: Systematic analysis of functional 3’ UTR genetic variants and their relevance to Alzheimer’s Disease
text:
Post-transcriptional regulation can significantly alter gene expression and contribute to
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) mechanisms. The proposed research aims to combine bioinformatic
and experimental methods to study functional genetic mutations or polymorphisms that cause
post-transcriptional changes in AD. This work will provide mechanistic basis for how genetic
variations may contribute to AD, such that future interventions can target specific genes
therapeutically.

title: Research Program: Immune Regulation Targets (IRT)
text: IMMUNE CELL REGULATION AND TARGETING PROGRAM (IRT) The Immune Cell Regulation and Targeting (IRT) Program investigates the role of adaptive and innate immune cells in cancer development and progression with a translational focus on identifying targetable mechanisms in lymphoid and myeloid cells and developing new approaches to improve cancer immunotherapy. The aims of the IRT Program are to: 1) Determine immune cell functions that shape the tumor immune environment and impact cancer development and progression; 2) Identify targetable mechanisms of lymphoid and myeloid malignancy development and survival, and new strategies to improve treatment; and 3) Develop new methods and strategies to harness and improve immune cell targeting of cancers for therapeutic intervention. Through transdisciplinary research that bridges multiple immune-based approaches and cancer types, IRT drives the Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center’s mission to bring cutting-edge cancer immunotherapies to its catchment area, with an emphasis on priority cancers, such as colon, and multiple myeloma. The IRT Program excels in combining research on immune cells and novel immunotherapies with training the next generation of nresearchers by employing multiple teaching and mentoring modalities and supporting career development and funding opportunities at all levels. Community outreach by IRT members through a variety of avenues leads to bidirectional education, improving IRT members’ understanding of the population in the catchment area, conveying the benefits of the center’s research to our communities, and learning from our community what is important to them. The IRT Program is led by Christine Eischen, PhD, and Pierluigi Porcu, MD, who provide complementary expertise in the molecular mechanisms of cancer initiation and survival, and clinical trials and targeted therapies in hematologic malignancies, respectively. To capture the research strengths across the consortium, the Program assembles 45 members from 14 departments across Thomas Jefferson University and Drexel University. IRT members have successfully published high-impact papers and obtained both federal and non-federal grant support. Total cancer relevant funding is $17.5 M with $1.8 M from NCI and a further $6.3 M from other NIH institutes and DOD. IRT has published 725 cancer-relevant research articles of which 20% are intra-programmatic, 18.9% are inter-programmatic, and 41.4% are collaborative with other NCI-designated Cancer Centers. Important discoveries have been published in high-impact journals including N Engl J Med, Cancer Discov, J Clin Invest, Nat Commun, Blood, Nat Med, and Clin Cancer Res. The IRT Program’s future directions are aligned to the Sidney Kimmel Cancer Center strategic plan, IMPACT PHL. Future goals are to: 1) Significantly expand tumor immunology and immune cell-based research; 2) Develop programmatic research in lymphoid and myeloid malignancies; and 3) Broaden and deepen the productive partnership between population science and IRT investigators.

title: Cellular and molecular regulators of melanocyte regeneration
text:
Melanocyte regeneration is important for the homeostasis and repair of pigmented skin. This proposal seeks to
identify and characterize genetic and cellular factors that guide melanocyte regeneration, both by identifying
and characterizing human melanocyte stem cells and utilizing the advantages of functional analyses available
in the zebrafish system. The knowledge gained from these studies aims to positively impact treatment of
individuals with pigmentary disorders, including the 0.2-1.8% of the world’s population with vitiligo.

title: Investigating the molecular mechanisms underlying sleep disruption in Smith-Kingsmore Syndrome
text:
Smith-Kingsmore Syndrome (SKS) is a rare and debilitating neurodevelopmental disorder caused by
hyperactivating mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) mutations, leading to clinically variable symptoms
including sleep disruption, body temperature dysregulation, intellectual disability, seizures, and megalencephaly.
The proposed research will use Drosophila models of SKS to investigate how different SKS variants affect mTOR
activity, circadian clock function, and mitochondrial homeostasis in the brain. Results from this work will inform
future therapeutic strategies for SKS and will advance our broader understanding of how mTOR dysregulation
contributes to neurological symptoms.

title: Selective autophagy mediated by TRIM proteins
text:
Autophagy is a mechanism of cellular waste removal that selectively identifies and eliminates unwanted and
potentially dangerous cellular contents including damaged organelles, toxic protein aggregates, or invading
microorganisms. The goal of this project is to gain a fundamental understanding of how the autophagy
machinery identifies its targets for elimination. This understanding is required for the possible development of
therapies that could selectively activate or inhibit certain types of autophagy to promote health while leaving
others unperturbed to minimize off-target effects.

title: Using Machine Learning to Predict Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Risk from Electronic Health Records
text:
Early detection of abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) is key to preventing deadly aortic ruptures. Our
research focuses on improving AAA diagnosis by externally validating current methods, using advanced
computer vision and machine learning to diagnose AAA from electronic health records, and refining screening
strategies to make them more effective for large populations. This study will improve AAA detection in men, set
new best practices for using artificial intelligence in cardiovascular disease diagnosis, and provide women—
who are not currently included in screening recommendations—better diagnostic options.

title: Autophagic Processes and Hepatocellular Steatosis
text:
Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is characterized by excessive fat
accumulation in the liver that is strongly associated with metabolic disorders, diabetes, and liver
inflammation/failure. As the US incidence of MASLD has increased significantly in the past decade (>30%), the
goal of this proposal is aimed at understanding the cellular and molecular basis by which the hepatocyte, the
major functional cell of the liver, normally breaks down fat stores (called lipid droplets, LDs) for energy
production. This process appears to be compromised in steatotic livers; therefore, this proposal will provide
new mechanistic insights required for treatment of MASLD.

title: Elucidating the Role of Cancer-Associated FGL1 in Tumor Immunity and Developing FGL1-Guided Anti-LAG-3 Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
This proposal seeks to elucidate the immune-suppressive mechanism of FGL1, a novel LAG-3 functional ligand,
on the regulation of T cell responses in the tumor microenvironment and explore its prognostic value in cancer
immunotherapy. We will also characterize a series of new antibodies targeting LAG-3 that differentially block
either or both FGL1/MHC-II ligands, both functionally and structurally, and explore better approaches targeting
the LAG-3 pathway in the control of tumor immunity for clinical application. The successful completion of our
proposed studies will provide important insights into FGL1/LAG-3 cancer immunobiology and suggest new
approaches for next-generation cancer immunotherapies.

title: Advancing cancer vaccine design using deep learning to predict peptide-HLA class I binding and immunogenicity
text:
Melanoma is a highly aggressive form of skin cancer, and despite advancements in immune checkpoint
blockade therapies, many patients still fail to respond or have durable remission. Cancer vaccines can serve
as a personalized treatment option, and this proposal seeks to improve vaccine design by employing machine
learning models to better predict peptide-HLA binding and model immunogenicity using peptide-HLA complex
stability. This work will refine peptide selection for cancer vaccines in ongoing trials and inform therapeutic
strategies to enhance clinical outcomes for future patients.

title: Dartmouth Training Program in Quantitative Cancer Research
text:
Support is requested for a multidisciplinary predoctoral Dartmouth Training program in
Quantitative Cancer Research. It is our vision that the next generation of quantitative
researchers will require skills and expertise from areas such as bioinformatics, biostatistics, and
epidemiology to tackle the most challenging problems in future cancer research.

title: Systems-to-structure approaches for defining mitochondrial protein function
text:
Mitochondria are home to a wide array of metabolic process and their dysfunction is implicated in many rare and
common human disease. However, the nature and cause of mitochondrial dysfunction is often unclear in large
part due to the fact that hundreds of mitochondrial proteins have unclear functions. The long-term goal of this
proposal is to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of mitochondrial biology and pathophysiology by
systematically defining the functions of orphan mitochondrial proteins and their roles within disease-related
processes.

title: Machine learning discovery of novel brainstem nuclei controlling orofacial behaviors
text:
This proposal will benefit public health by revealing the structure and function of brain regions involved in control
of orofacial behaviors, such as making facial expressions, breathing, swallowing, chewing, and vocalization, in
health and disease. Identifying these regions will permit development of therapies for conditions affecting the
brainstem where these movements are impaired and help improve the availability and reduce the risk of surgical
brainstem procedures.

title: 2026 Immunometabolism in Health and Disease Gordon Research Conference and Gordon Research Seminar
text:
The 2026 Gordon Research Conference (GRC) and Seminar (GRS) on Immunometabolism in Health and
Disease will bring together international experts, early-stage investigators, and trainees to explore emerging
concepts at the intersection of cellular metabolism and immune function. The program will address the
mechanistic roles of metabolism in myeloid and lymphoid cells and their therapeutic relevance across a broad
range of immune-mediated diseases, including infection, allergy, autoimmunity, cancer, atherosclerosis, obesity,
and diabetes. The GRC and GRS will also foster collaboration between academia and industry while supporting
the development of the next generation of scientists in this rapidly growing interdisciplinary field.

title: Ion Channel Transporter Interactions
text:
Ion channels pass electrical currents in the form of charged ions and are essential for processes as diverse as
the heartbeat, thought, and movement. This project will define new paradigms in ion channel function involving
regulation of ion channels by solute transporters (and vice versa) and small molecules and uncover new roles
for ion channels in health and disease. These studies will ultimately help produce better therapeutic approaches
to treat disorders including epilepsy, pain, inflammation, ataxia, and hypertension.

title: TR&D3
text: D Cai and K Najarian will serve as Project Lead and co-Lead, respectively, for TRD3. Live fluorescence imaging is challenged by high levels of autofluorescence background and potential for photobleaching and phototoxicity. Faster frame rates are needed to capture subtle cellular behaviors, but an increase in imaging speed may result in a reduction of signal. TRD3 will develop properly trained machine-leaning models that can effectively denoise images captured with at least 5 times higher frame rates. Importantly, a faster frame rate can significantly mitigate motion artifacts, which is critical to interpret images collected in vivo and track biological processes. Environmental perturbations and movement can blur individual images, and substantially degrade the usefulness of video streams. Microendoscopy is especially sensitive to motion because the image field-of-view is typically only a few hundred microns in dimensions. Image segmentation remains one of the most challenging tasks in biomedical image processing, in particular, at the cellular level. Live imaging normally results in uneven intensity distributions, noise patterns, weak edges, and frequently incomplete features. Rapid advances in the deep learning field has dramatically improved the accuracy of feature extraction from in vivo fluorescence images using complex illumination and noise conditions, and have increased in popularity with the development of massive parallel computing architectures. These algorithms can enable precise image recognition based on high-dimensional hierarchical image features. Deep learning algorithms can be trained using validated clinical datasets to provide real time digital readouts. In vivo cellular activity visualized using microendoscopy will be correlated with their molecular properties via postmortem tissue imaging. This approach allows for the dynamic behaviors of live cells visualized in vivo, and compared with mRNA and protein expression to identify upregulated signaling pathways. Valuable insights into cellular function and behaviors can be used to elucidate physiological mechanisms. Morphological profiles that are versatile descriptors of biological systems can be generated and used to predict in vitro and in vivo drug effects. New drugs can be developed, and their potential impact can be better understood. CP/SPs are currently performing live imaging and molecular profiling separately using different sets of animals. Scientific conclusions are drawn from statistical averages calculated from different cohorts. The number of experimental animals needed to draw significant conclusions can be substantially reduced, and uncertainties introduced by individual differences in statistical analysis can be minimized. TRD3 will support CP/SPs to advance their scientific discoveries with higher accuracy and confidence. Synergy: TRD3 will use in vivo optical sections collected by TRD2 to develop machine learning models for automated digital pathology, and will quantify tumor dimensions to assess therapeutic efficacy using photoacoustic images collected with microsystems sensors developed in TRD1.

title: A Multimodal Assessment Protocol for Characterizing Restricted and Repetitive Behaviors in Autism
text:
Scalable, multi-method, comprehensive assessments of restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB) are
essential for enhancing the pathways from screening and characterization to treatment tailoring and tracking
of these clinically impactful symptoms in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The overarching
aim of the proposed project is to develop and validate novel, multimodal, scalable, time- and cost-efficient
assessment protocols for comprehensive characterization of key RRB subdomains that can assist in the
diagnostic process, facilitating etiologically oriented research, the treatment selection, and monitoring
symptomatology over time. This project will yield the world’s first comprehensive RRB assessment
ecosystem that incorporates state-of-the-art psychometric principles and will have the potential to
significantly advance the characterization and tracking of key types of RRB across clinical and research
contexts.
